title: Blockchain Architecture & Networks
tagline: Design the whole system: nodes, state, scaling, bridges, oracles and dApp layers, with calculators and design labs
summary: A design-focused course on how blockchain systems are built: peer-to-peer networks and node types, state and storage, scaling with rollups and channels, bridges and oracles, the layers of a decentralised app, and how to choose and record architecture decisions. Spreadsheet and explorer labs let you calculate throughput, storage, rollup savings and availability.

modules.title: Peer-to-peer networks and nodes
modules.summary: How thousands of computers find each other, share blocks and keep one network running with no central server.
modules.outcome: You can describe peer-to-peer networking, name node types and explain how a block spreads by gossip.
modules.intro: A blockchain is only as good as the network that carries it. This module opens the networking layer: how nodes find each other, what different kinds of node do, and why a network without a central server can still be fast and robust.

topics.title: Peer-to-peer versus client-server
topics.html:
Two architectures
Client-serverPeer-to-peer (P2P)
StructureMany clients talk to one central serverEvery node can talk to many others
FailureIf the server fails, the service failsIndividual nodes can fail without stopping the network
ControlThe operator controls rules and dataRules are in software every node runs
ScalingThe operator must add capacityCapacity grows as nodes join, but coordination is harder
ExamplesA banking website, a streaming serviceFile-sharing networks, Bitcoin and Ethereum

In a blockchain network each node is both a client and a server: it requests data from peers and serves data to them. There is no leader to phone. Instead, every node follows the same rules, checks what it receives and forwards what is valid.

Check what you just learned

1. What happens when one node in a peer-to-peer network fails?
  • The whole network stops
  • The leader is replaced
  • All data is lost
  • Other nodes keep running (correct)

There is no single point of failure.

Tip

A node never has to trust a peer's word. It checks the data itself. That is why 'don't trust, verify' is a slogan of the field.

Check what you just learned

1. In a P2P blockchain network each node:
  • Is both a client and a server (correct)
  • Only requests data
  • Is controlled by a central bank
  • Only stores wallets

It asks and serves.
keyPoints: P2P networks have no central server; every node can be client and server.
Nodes verify everything they receive before forwarding it.

topics.title: Types of node
topics.html:
Common node types
NodeWhat it stores and checksResourcesTypical user
Full nodeEvery block and the current state; verifies all rulesModerate to highExchanges, services, enthusiasts
Light clientBlock headers; asks others for proofs of what it needsLowPhone wallets
Archive nodeEverything a full node has, plus every historical stateVery highBlock explorers, analytics
Validator or mining nodeA full node that also takes part in consensusHigh, plus staked funds or hardwareBlock producers
RPC or gateway nodeA full node exposed to apps via an APIHighInfrastructure providers

The more you rely on other people's nodes, the more you trust them. A light client that asks a company's server for balances is trusting that company not to lie, unless it also checks proofs. Running your own full node is the strongest way to verify the network for yourself.

Watch out

Many apps use a single hosted node provider. If it goes down, or serves wrong data, the app breaks. Good architectures use more than one provider and verify what matters.

Check what you just learned

1. Which node type stores every historical state of the chain?
  • Light client
  • Archive node (correct)
  • Full node
  • Validator

Archive nodes keep everything, which is very large.

Check what you just learned

1. A phone wallet that checks block headers and Merkle proofs is a:
  • Full node
  • Archive node
  • Light client (correct)
  • Miner

It stays light by verifying only what it needs.
keyPoints: Full, light, archive, validator and RPC nodes make different trade-offs.
Relying on others' nodes means trusting them.

topics.title: Discovery, gossip and client diversity
topics.html:
A new node starts knowing only a few addresses (bootstrap nodes) published in the software. It asks them for the addresses of more peers, and soon has a list of dozens. It then keeps connections open to some of them and exchanges messages.

Definition

Gossip protocol. A way of spreading information in which each node tells a few randomly chosen peers, who each tell a few more, so a message reaches the whole network in a small number of rounds.

How many rounds to reach everyone?

Change the number of nodes and the fanout (how many peers each informed node tells per round). The number of rounds grows only slowly with the size of the network.

Adjust Number of nodes, Fanout (peers told per node per round) and see Rounds needed (about), Nodes informed after 3 rounds (about) change.

Why client diversity matters

  • If everyone runs the same software, one bug can stop or split the whole network.
  • Ethereum, for example, encourages several independent implementations of both its execution and consensus clients.
  • Operators should avoid running the majority client, so that one bug cannot affect most of the network.
  • More implementations also test the written specification better.

Check what you just learned

1. Why does gossip reach a huge network in few rounds?
  • Each node tells everyone at once
  • Messages travel at light speed
  • A central server relays it
  • The number of informed nodes multiplies each round (correct)

Growth is exponential.

Check what you just learned

1. A bootstrap node is:
  • A known address a new node uses to find peers (correct)
  • A startup coin
  • A kind of block
  • A wallet

The first step into the network.

Key terms: flip and sort

Peer-to-peer
A network where nodes talk directly to each other
Full node
A node that verifies all rules and keeps the state
Light client
A node that checks headers and proofs only
Archive node
A node that keeps all historical state
Gossip
Spreading data by telling random peers
Client diversity
Several independent software implementations
keyPoints: Nodes find peers through bootstrap nodes and spread data by gossip.
Software diversity protects against single bugs.

modules.title: Data, state and storage
modules.summary: What a chain stores, how state is organised and what belongs on-chain versus off-chain.
modules.outcome: You can distinguish the ledger from the state, estimate storage growth and decide what data to place on a chain.
modules.intro: A blockchain is a history, but applications need answers about the present: who owns what right now. This module separates the two, shows how nodes manage both, and gives you a rule for placing data.

topics.title: Ledger versus state
topics.html:
Definition

State. The current picture produced by applying every transaction in order: balances, contract storage, who owns which token. A node keeps the state so it can check new transactions quickly.

History and state
Ledger (history)State (present)
ContainsEvery block and transaction since the startThe result of applying all of them
ChangesOnly grows by appendingUpdated by every block
Needed toAudit and replayValidate new transactions fast
SizeGrows without endGrows with the number of accounts and contracts

On account-based chains the state is organised as a tree of hashes (in Ethereum, a Merkle Patricia trie). The root of that tree is written into each block header, so a single value commits to every balance and every contract's storage. A light client can verify one account's balance with a short proof against that root.

A small tree, a changing root

Imagine each leaf is an account's balance. Edit one and see how the root changes. This is the idea behind committing to the whole state with one value.

4 transactions are hashed in pairs up to one Merkle root. Change one transaction and the root changes.

Check what you just learned

1. What does a node keep so it can validate new transactions quickly?
  • Only block headers
  • The current state (correct)
  • Paper copies
  • A password

State answers 'who owns what now'.

Check what you just learned

1. The state root in a block header lets a light client:
  • Mine blocks
  • Change history
  • Verify an account's balance with a short proof (correct)
  • Set fees

A Merkle proof against the root.
keyPoints: State is the present picture; the ledger is the history.
A hash of the state is committed in each block header.

topics.title: Storage growth and syncing
topics.html:
Because history only grows, chains get bigger every day. That raises the cost of running a node, which can reduce decentralisation if only well-funded operators can afford it. Designers use several tools to manage growth.

Ways to manage growth
TechniqueWhat it doesTrade-off
PruningDeletes old data that is no longer needed to validate new blocksA pruned node cannot serve old history
Snapshot or snap syncDownload a recent verified state instead of replaying everythingYou trust the checkpoint's proof or the community
Statelessness and state expiryResearch ideas to reduce how much state each node must holdComplex changes to the protocol
Light clientsVerify only what they needDepend on full nodes for data
Limits on block size and gasCap growth per blockCaps throughput

Chain growth calculator

Change the block time and average block size to see how much data a chain adds per year.

Adjust Block time (seconds), Average block size (kilobytes) and see Blocks per day, Data added per year (GB) change.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is fast-growing storage a decentralisation risk?
  • Because disks are free
  • Because hashes shrink
  • Because blocks vanish
  • Because only well-funded operators may afford to run nodes (correct)

Higher costs mean fewer independent nodes.

Check what you just learned

1. Pruning means:
  • Deleting old data no longer needed for validation (correct)
  • Adding blocks
  • Mining
  • Fees

A pruned node keeps less history.
keyPoints: Chains grow forever; pruning, snapshots and limits manage the cost.
High node costs reduce decentralisation.

topics.title: What belongs on-chain?
topics.html:
On-chain storage is slow, replicated everywhere, public and expensive. That makes it ideal for small facts everyone must agree on, and a poor choice for bulky or private data.

A placement guide
Keep on-chainKeep off-chain
Ownership and balancesImages, video and documents
Rules enforced by contractsPersonal and private data
Hashes (fingerprints) of documentsAnything that changes constantly
Small commitments such as a Merkle rootLogs, analytics and large datasets
Definition

Content addressing (IPFS). A way of naming files by the hash of their content instead of by a location. If the file changes, its name changes, so a link is also a tamper check. Systems such as IPFS use this, but a file stays available only while someone keeps hosting ('pinning') it.

A file's name is its fingerprint

Type some text. In content addressing, this fingerprint, not a web address, would be the file's name.

Type any text and see its SHA-256 fingerprint change completely when one letter changes.

Common mistakes

  • Storing personal data on a public chain, where it cannot be deleted.
  • Assuming a file linked from an NFT will exist forever.
  • Putting large data on-chain just because you can.

Check what you just learned

1. Where should a scanned passport be stored in a credential system?
  • On a public blockchain
  • Off-chain under privacy controls, with at most a hash on-chain (correct)
  • In a smart contract
  • In a token name

A chain cannot delete personal data.

Check what you just learned

1. A hash stored on-chain for a document proves:
  • The document is true
  • The document is secret
  • The document existed unchanged at that time (correct)
  • The document is large

It proves integrity, not truth.

Key terms: flip and sort

State
The current picture produced by all transactions
State root
A hash committing to the whole state
Pruning
Deleting old data not needed for validation
Snapshot sync
Starting from a recent verified state
Content addressing
Naming data by its hash
Pinning
Hosting a file so it stays available
keyPoints: On-chain: small, shared, public facts. Off-chain: big or private data.
Content addressing names data by its hash.

steps: List ten pieces of data it needs.
Explain any hash you will store.

modules.title: Performance and scaling
modules.summary: Throughput, latency and cost, and the main techniques for scaling: rollups, channels, sharding and sidechains.
modules.outcome: You can estimate throughput and cost, compare optimistic and ZK rollups and choose a scaling approach for a use case.
modules.intro: A chain that everyone wants to use quickly becomes slow and expensive. Scaling is the set of techniques that let more people use a system without sacrificing the security that made it worth using.

topics.title: Throughput, latency and cost
topics.html:
Three measures
MeasureMeaningDepends on
ThroughputTransactions processed per secondBlock size, block time, transaction size
LatencyTime from sending until includedBlock time, congestion, fee level
Finality timeTime until a transaction is practically irreversibleConsensus mechanism
CostWhat a user pays per transactionDemand for block space, computation used
Formula · Throughput

tps = (block size ÷ average transaction size) ÷ block time

A 100 KB block of 200-byte transactions holds 500 transactions; at 12 seconds per block that is about 42 per second.

Throughput calculator

Change block size, transaction size and block time to see throughput. Notice the limits of simply making blocks bigger.

Adjust Block size (kilobytes), Average transaction (bytes), Block time (seconds) and see Transactions per block, Transactions per second change.

Raising throughput by enlarging blocks or shortening block time has side effects: bigger blocks take longer to spread and need better hardware, which can push small operators out. That is the scalability side of the trilemma.

Check what you just learned

1. Which change would raise throughput directly?
  • Smaller blocks
  • More fees
  • Larger transactions
  • Shorter block time (correct)

More blocks per second means more transactions.

Check what you just learned

1. Latency is:
  • Time until a transaction is included (correct)
  • Transactions per second
  • Fees
  • Block size

How long you wait.
keyPoints: Throughput, latency, finality and cost are different measures.
Bigger and faster blocks help throughput but strain decentralisation.

topics.title: Layer 2: rollups and channels
topics.html:
Definition

Rollup. A layer-2 system that executes many transactions off the base chain, then posts a compact record of them (and a proof or a way to challenge them) to the base chain, so the base chain's security protects the results.

Two kinds of rollup
Optimistic rollupZK rollup
How correctness is ensuredAssume valid; anyone can submit a fraud proof during a challenge windowA validity proof (a zero-knowledge proof) shows the batch was computed correctly
Withdrawal to the base chainCan take days because of the challenge period (unless a liquidity provider speeds it up)Fast once the proof is verified
ComplexitySimpler to build, supports existing programs wellCryptographically heavy; support for general programs has been maturing
CostPosting data to the base chain dominatesProof generation adds work, but proofs are small to verify

State channels work differently: two parties lock funds on-chain, then exchange signed updates off-chain as many times as they like, and settle only the final result. They are fast and cheap between fixed participants but not suited to open-ended interaction. Sidechains are separate chains with their own validators, linked by bridges; their security does not come from the base chain.

Rollup savings

Change how many transactions share a batch and see the cost per transaction. Teaching figures.

Adjust Cost to post a batch (rupees), Transactions per batch, Rollup fee per transaction (rupees), Cost of a direct base-layer transaction (rupees) and see Rollup cost per transaction, Times cheaper than direct change.

Check what you just learned

1. Why can withdrawals from an optimistic rollup take days?
  • Because of banking hours
  • To leave time for fraud proofs to be submitted (correct)
  • Because proofs are slow to generate
  • Because of block size

The challenge window protects against fraud.

Check what you just learned

1. A state channel settles on-chain:
  • Every transaction
  • Never
  • Only the final result (correct)
  • Hourly

Updates happen off-chain.
keyPoints: Rollups batch transactions and rely on the base layer for security.
Optimistic rollups use fraud proofs; ZK rollups use validity proofs.

topics.title: Sharding, data availability and choosing
topics.html:
Sharding splits the network's work or data into pieces handled by different groups, so not every node processes everything. It raises capacity but adds complexity, especially for transactions that touch several shards. Ethereum's current direction favours scaling through rollups and cheaper data space for them (introduced in 2024 as 'blobs') rather than splitting execution.

Definition

Data availability. The guarantee that the data behind a block or batch was actually published, so anyone can check it or rebuild the state. Without it, a block producer could hide data and make verification impossible.

Choosing a scaling approach
NeedLikely fit
Open, general-purpose apps with security from a strong base chainRollups
Frequent payments between two or a few known partiesState channels
A separate app-specific chain with its own validator setSidechain or app chain
A consortium of known organisationsA permissioned chain, scaled by hardware and design
Very small user numbersNo scaling needed: the base chain is enough
Watch out

Faster and cheaper usually means trusting something more: a smaller validator set, a bridge, a prover or a sequencer. Ask what new assumptions a scaling solution adds.

Check what you just learned

1. What does 'data availability' guarantee?
  • Data is secret
  • Data is free
  • Data is small
  • Data behind a block was actually published for verification (correct)

Hidden data cannot be checked.

Check what you just learned

1. Which usually needs the fewest extra trust assumptions?
  • A rollup with proofs posted to the base chain (correct)
  • A sidechain with five validators
  • An unaudited bridge
  • A private server

It inherits base-layer security.

Key terms: flip and sort

Throughput
Transactions per second
Latency
Time until inclusion
Rollup
Layer 2 that posts compact data to a base chain
Fraud proof
A challenge showing an invalid batch
Validity proof
A proof that a batch is correct
Data availability
Guarantee that data was published
keyPoints: Sharding splits work; rollups scale by batching.
Every scaling choice adds trust assumptions to examine.

modules.title: Interoperability and oracles
modules.summary: How chains talk to each other and to the outside world, and why both are among the riskiest parts of any design.
modules.outcome: You can compare bridge designs by trust assumptions and design a basic oracle with redundancy.
modules.intro: Blockchains are closed worlds: they know only what is written on them. To be useful, they must exchange value with other chains and learn facts about the real world. Both connections have proved to be among the most attacked parts of the ecosystem.

topics.title: Bridges and cross-chain messaging
topics.html:
A bridge lets assets or messages move between chains. Because one chain cannot read another directly, a bridge adds something in the middle, and that something must be trusted.

Common bridge designs
DesignHow it worksWhat you must trust
Lock and mintAssets are locked on chain A; a wrapped copy is minted on chain BWhoever controls the lock and the minting
Burn and releaseWrapped tokens are burned on B and released on AThe same
Multi-signature or committee bridgeA group signs transfersThat a majority of signers is honest and secure
Light-client bridgeA contract verifies the other chain's block headersThe code and the other chain's security
Liquidity networkProviders hold funds on both sides and swap for a feeThe providers and the relay system
Watch out

Bridges hold large pools of locked assets, which makes them attractive targets, and several bridge hacks have each lost hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of assets. Moving funds across a bridge adds risk that the underlying chains do not have.

Check what you just learned

1. In a lock-and-mint bridge, what backs the wrapped token on the destination chain?
  • Nothing
  • The original asset locked on the source chain (correct)
  • A bank
  • Mining

If the lock is stolen the wrapped token is unbacked.

Tip

Prefer fewer hops and well-audited bridges, and avoid keeping large amounts in wrapped assets longer than you need.

Check what you just learned

1. A wrapped token is:
  • A gas fee
  • A paper note
  • A token that represents an asset locked elsewhere (correct)
  • A wallet

Its value depends on the lock.
keyPoints: A bridge needs someone or something trusted to relay and hold assets.
Bridge hacks are among the largest losses in the field.

topics.title: Oracles: bringing the world on-chain
topics.html:
Definition

Oracle. A service that delivers off-chain data to a smart contract, such as a price, a weather reading or the result of a match. Because contracts act automatically, a wrong oracle value can cause real losses.

Oracle design choices
ChoiceWeak designStronger design
SourcesOne data providerSeveral independent providers
AggregationUse the latest single valueUse the median or a trimmed average
OperatorsOne nodeMany independent nodes with signed reports
TimelinessAccept any old valueReject stale data and check update times
ManipulationUse one thinly traded market's priceUse deep, multiple markets and time-weighted averages

Median beats one bad source

Three sources report a price. Change one to a wildly wrong value and compare the average with the median.

Adjust Source A, Source B, Source C (try a bad value) and see Average of the three, Median of the three change.

Common mistakes

  • Using one exchange's spot price as a contract's source of truth.
  • Ignoring how long ago the data was updated.
  • Trusting an oracle with unlimited power over funds, instead of adding limits and a pause.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use the median of several sources?
  • It is easier
  • It is cheaper
  • It is slower
  • One wrong source cannot decide the value (correct)

It resists a single bad input.

Check what you just learned

1. The oracle problem is:
  • Getting trustworthy real-world data onto a chain (correct)
  • Slow blocks
  • High fees
  • Lost keys

Contracts cannot check the world themselves.
keyPoints: Oracles feed off-chain facts to contracts and are a major risk.
Use several sources, the median and checks on freshness.

topics.title: Designing with these risks
topics.html:
Defensive habits

  1. Limit how much value passes through any one bridge or oracle.
  2. Add circuit breakers: a pause that stops the system if prices or flows look abnormal.
  3. Rate-limit withdrawals so that a single exploit cannot drain everything at once.
  4. Keep contracts simple, audited and monitored.
  5. Plan an incident response: who can pause, and how do users learn about it?
  6. Publish clearly what the system trusts.
Questions to ask about any external dependency
QuestionWhy it matters
Who can change the data or the code?That party can attack the system
What happens if it stops working?Availability risk
How would I know if it were wrong?Detection
What is the most that could be lost?Sets limits

Check what you just learned

1. What is a circuit breaker in a contract system?
  • A hardware part
  • A pause that halts operations when something looks wrong (correct)
  • A fee
  • A wallet feature

It limits damage in an incident.

Check what you just learned

1. Rate-limiting withdrawals helps by:
  • Raising fees
  • Speeding up blocks
  • Limiting how much an exploit can drain at once (correct)
  • Hiding balances

It buys time to respond.

Key terms: flip and sort

Bridge
A system moving assets or messages between chains
Wrapped token
A token representing an asset locked elsewhere
Oracle
A source of off-chain data for contracts
Median
The middle value of a set
Circuit breaker
A mechanism that pauses a system
Attack surface
All the ways a system can be attacked
keyPoints: Limit exposure, add pauses and rate limits, and publish trust assumptions.
Every external dependency is an attack surface.

modules.title: Architecture of a dApp
modules.summary: How a real decentralised application is assembled from a front end, wallet, node access, smart contracts and off-chain services.
modules.outcome: You can draw and explain the layers of a dApp, say what belongs in each and describe failure modes and mitigations.
modules.intro: Most decentralised applications are hybrids: part on a blockchain, part in ordinary web infrastructure. Knowing exactly where the boundary is, and what each side must never do, is what separates a robust design from a fragile one.

topics.title: The layers
topics.html:
What each layer does
LayerJobMust never
Front endShows data, builds transactions for the user to reviewHold private keys or hide what a transaction does
WalletHolds keys and signs after the user approvesSign without showing the user what it is signing
RPC providerSends transactions and reads chain dataBe the only source of truth for important checks
Smart contractsEnforce the rules and hold assetsRely on unverified off-chain input
IndexerReads events and builds fast queriesBe the authority for balances; the chain is
Off-chain servicesEmail, QR codes, KYC, analyticsHold the ability to move user funds
StorageLarge files and metadataContain secrets or personal data without protection

Check what you just learned

1. Which layer holds the user's private keys?
  • Front end
  • Indexer
  • RPC provider
  • Wallet (correct)

The wallet signs; apps never see keys.

Check what you just learned

1. An indexer is used to:
  • Build fast queries from on-chain events (correct)
  • Mine blocks
  • Store keys
  • Pay fees

Reading raw chain data is slow.
keyPoints: Front end, wallet, RPC, contracts, indexer, off-chain services and storage each have a clear job.
Keys stay in the wallet; the chain is the source of truth.

topics.title: A request from click to confirmation
topics.html:
Notice that the front end does not 'know' the purchase succeeded just because it sent the transaction. It must wait for confirmation and read the result from the chain or from an indexer that follows it. Good apps show clear states: waiting for signature, sent, confirmed, failed.

What can go wrong at each step
StepFailureMitigation
WalletUser rejectsShow a friendly message; allow retry
BroadcastFee too low; network congestionOffer fee options and a 'speed up' option
ExecutionThe contract revertsShow the reason; simulate before sending
ConfirmationA reorganisation drops the blockWait for sufficient confirmations for high-value actions
IndexerLag or outageFall back to reading the chain directly
Tip

Simulate a transaction before asking the user to sign. A failed transaction still costs fees, and a clear error helps the user avoid wasting money.

Check what you just learned

1. Why should a front end simulate a transaction first?
  • To make it slower
  • To catch failures before the user pays fees (correct)
  • To hide it from the wallet
  • To reduce block size

Failures cost gas.

Check what you just learned

1. A transaction that is sent but not yet confirmed is:
  • Final
  • Deleted
  • Pending and could still fail (correct)
  • Reversed

Wait for confirmation.
keyPoints: Show clear transaction states: signing, sent, confirmed, failed.
Simulate before sending to avoid wasted fees.

topics.title: Reliability, upgrades and cost
topics.html:
Reliability habits

  1. Use more than one RPC provider, with automatic fallback.
  2. Keep the front end available on more than one host, and publish the contract addresses.
  3. Monitor contract events and balances, with alerts for anything unusual.
  4. Write a status page and an incident plan.
  5. Test on a test network and on a fork of the main network before deploying.
  6. Cache and index to keep the interface fast.
Upgrading contracts
ApproachWhat it meansTrade-off
Immutable contractsCode cannot change after deploymentStrongest promise to users; bugs cannot be fixed in place
Upgradable proxiesA proxy contract forwards calls to a logic contract that can be replacedFixes are possible, but whoever can upgrade holds great power
Governed upgradesUpgrades need a vote or a time-lockSlower, more transparent

The value of a backup provider

Change the reliability of one provider and how many you use to see the chance the app is fully down.

Adjust Availability of one provider (%), Number of independent providers and see Chance all providers are down, Combined availability (%) change.

Watch out

An upgradable contract is only as trustworthy as the keys or votes that control the upgrade. Users should be able to see who holds that power and what delay applies.

Check what you just learned

1. An upgradable proxy contract lets the owner:
  • Hide balances
  • Delete the chain
  • Mine blocks
  • Change the logic the proxy calls (correct)

Which is powerful and must be governed.

Key terms: flip and sort

dApp
A decentralised application
RPC
Remote procedure call: how apps talk to nodes
Indexer
A service that organises on-chain events for fast queries
Proxy
A contract that forwards calls to replaceable logic
Time-lock
A delay before a change takes effect
Simulation
Running a transaction without sending it for real
keyPoints: Redundancy, monitoring and incident plans keep a dApp reliable.
Upgradability trades fixability for trust in whoever can upgrade.

modules.title: Making design decisions
modules.summary: Choosing a network type, a platform and a design, and recording why.
modules.outcome: You can choose between public, consortium and private networks, evaluate platforms with criteria and write an architecture decision record.
modules.intro: The best architects are not those who know the most technologies but those who can explain why one fits. This module teaches a decision method and gives you practice writing proposals and decisions.

topics.title: Public, consortium or private?
topics.html:
Three network types
Public permissionlessConsortium (permissioned)Private
Who can joinAnyoneApproved membersOne organisation
Who validatesOpen setKnown membersThe owner
Visibility of dataPublicMembers only (or selected)Internal
Speed and privacyLower speed, low privacy by defaultHigher speed, configurable privacyHighest
Trust modelCost and cryptographyGovernance and legal agreementsThe owner
Typical useOpen money, assets, public goodsIndustry networks such as trade finance and supply chainsInternal tools (often better served by a database)

A hybrid is common: a consortium keeps its detailed data on a permissioned network but periodically anchors a hash of its state to a public chain, so that outsiders can verify that the history was not rewritten.

Check what you just learned

1. A group of ten known banks sharing a settlement ledger most likely needs:
  • A consortium network (correct)
  • A public permissionless chain
  • No ledger
  • A game

Identified members and governance.

Check what you just learned

1. A private single-organisation 'blockchain' is often better replaced by:
  • A public chain
  • A normal database (correct)
  • A game
  • A token

Without shared control, a chain adds little.
keyPoints: Public, consortium and private networks suit different trust settings.
Anchoring a hash on a public chain can add outside verifiability.

topics.title: Evaluating platforms
topics.html:
Criteria and questions
CriterionQuestions
Security and maturityHow long has it run? What attacks has it survived? Are there independent audits?
DecentralisationHow many independent validators? How concentrated is stake or hash power?
Performance and costWhat are typical throughput, finality time and fees?
Tooling and ecosystemAre there good libraries, documentation, developers and auditors?
GovernanceWho decides changes? How are disputes resolved?
Legal and compliance fitDoes it work with privacy, tax and licensing rules in your market?
Exit optionsCan you move your data and contracts elsewhere if you must?

A weighted decision matrix

Weight security against cost and see which of two platforms scores better. Scores are 1 to 10.

Adjust Weight on security (%), Platform A security, Platform A low cost, Platform B security, Platform B low cost and see Platform A weighted score, Platform B weighted score change.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing a platform because of hype or a sponsor's discount.
  • Ignoring how hard it is to hire developers or auditors for it.
  • Not planning for the platform's failure or change of direction.

Check what you just learned

1. Which criterion is easy to overlook but important in the long run?
  • The logo
  • The founder's age
  • Exit options (correct)
  • Colour of the website

You may need to leave.

Check what you just learned

1. A weighted decision matrix helps you:
  • Hide the decision
  • Skip research
  • Pick randomly
  • Make trade-offs explicit (correct)

It shows what you value.
keyPoints: Judge platforms on security, decentralisation, cost, tooling, governance, legality and exit.
Use a weighted matrix and write down the weights.

topics.title: Writing decisions down
topics.html:
Definition

Architecture decision record (ADR). A short document recording an important design decision: the context, the options considered, the choice made and its consequences. It helps new team members, auditors and your future self understand why the system is the way it is.

Parts of an ADR
PartContent
ContextThe problem and constraints
OptionsAt least two or three realistic alternatives
DecisionThe choice and the main reasons
ConsequencesWhat gets easier, what gets harder, what risks remain
Status and dateProposed, accepted or replaced
Worked example

A short ADR

Where to store customers' scanned documents in a credential system.

  1. Context: privacy law requires that personal data can be deleted.
  2. Options: on-chain, IPFS, a regulated off-chain store with a hash on-chain.
  3. Decision: the off-chain store with the hash, because chains cannot delete data.
  4. Consequences: privacy rules can be met, but the system now depends on the store's security and availability.

Answer. A clear record turns a debate into a reviewable decision.

Habits of good architects

  • Write down the assumptions and test them.
  • Prefer the simplest design that meets the need.
  • Review designs with someone who will try to break them.
  • Revisit decisions when the context changes.

Check what you just learned

1. Why record the options you rejected?
  • So readers see what was considered and why it was not chosen (correct)
  • To fill space
  • Because law requires it
  • To make it longer

It shows the reasoning.

Check what you just learned

1. The consequences section of an ADR should include:
  • Only the benefits
  • Benefits, costs and remaining risks (correct)
  • A marketing slogan
  • Nothing

Be honest about trade-offs.

Key terms: flip and sort

Permissioned
Only approved participants take part
Consortium
A group of organisations sharing a network
Anchoring
Publishing a hash of data on another chain
Decision matrix
A table scoring options against criteria
ADR
Architecture decision record
Exit option
The ability to move away from a platform
keyPoints: An ADR records context, options, decision and consequences.
Simple, reviewed and revisited designs age best.
